---
title: "Methods and data sources"
---

## Glider data

The deployments are gridded (L3) NetCDF files produced by the NOAA Southwest Fisheries
Science Center (SWFSC) Ecosystem Science Division Glider Team with
[pyglider](https://github.com/c-proof/pyglider) and
[esdglider](https://github.com/SWFSC/esdglider)
([glider lab manual](https://swfsc.github.io/glider-lab-manual/)). Each file holds one
profile per column on 5 m depth bins, with one time, latitude and longitude per profile.
The data are in the public domain (CC0-1.0).

Values are shown as stored. The gridded QC flags are bin-averaged in these files, so they
are not used for masking. Potential density in the files was computed from raw,
uncorrected salinity.

Deployments without a local L3 file are downloaded from the
[IOOS Glider DAC ERDDAP](https://gliders.ioos.us/erddap/) and gridded the same way: each
profile's samples are averaged into 5 m depth bins. For a deployment available both ways
(calanus-20260824) this reproduced the L3 file to within 0.001 °C in every bin. Delayed-mode
data are used when published. Until then, real-time data are shown and labelled
**real-time (provisional)**: they are thinned, not quality-controlled and may have gaps. Each
deployment page and the Deployments table link to its ERDDAP dataset (deployments shown from local L3 files say "no ERDDAP dataset yet"). The site checks ERDDAP three times a day (scheduled for about 5:30 am, 11:30 am and 5:30 pm
Pacific, though GitHub often starts these runs late) and rebuilds
with any new or updated datasets; the date of the last check is shown on the home and
real-time pages. Deployments published from local L3 files are never replaced by their ERDDAP
versions unless listed in `erddap.json` in the site's repository.

**Variables.** Temperature, salinity, chlorophyll, oxygen, CDOM (coloured dissolved organic
matter, in the files' units, ppb) and optical backscatter at 700 nm (m⁻¹ sr⁻¹) are shown when
the deployment's file has data for them. Gliders carry different sensor packages: a variable
the file lacks, or holds no values for, gets no button in the viewer and is listed as
*not measured* on the deployment page. A variable recorded for fewer than 90% of a deployment's
profiles (for example, a sensor that failed part-way through) shows the share of profiles
that have it.

ERDDAP data are served by the U.S. IOOS Glider Data Assembly Center (DAC),
<https://gliders.ioos.us/>.

## What the viewer shows

**3D curtain.** The selected variable on a vertical surface beneath the glider track,
in km east/north of the deployment's mean position. Vertical exaggeration is adjustable;
land heights are scaled down so islands do not hide the curtain.

**Surface or points.** The curtain and the section can be drawn as a continuous surface or as
points (the *Curtain* control). Real-time data are thinned before transmission (for example,
samples about 10 m apart in the vertical for stenella-20261103), so many 5 m bins are empty, and
transmissions can pause for hours to more than a day. A surface drops every cell next to an empty
bin and is drawn straight across pauses. Real-time deployments therefore open as points, one per
sample as transmitted, at the sample's own time, depth and position; empty depths and pauses stay
blank, and the readout shows that sample's values. The T–S diagram and the derived quantities
(σθ, mixed-layer depth, chlorophyll maximum) still use the 5 m bins. Delayed-mode deployments
open as a surface; for them the points option shows one point per 5 m bin. Overlay lines (σθ
contours, mixed-layer depth, chlorophyll-max depth) are broken wherever profiles are more than
max(3 h, 4 × the median profile spacing) apart.

**Depth–time section.** The same variable against time and depth, with the seafloor
under the track, labelled σθ contours (lightly smoothed along time for display), and a
sun strip showing day, civil twilight, nautical twilight and night for each profile.

**T–S diagram.** Potential temperature against practical salinity for the selected date
window, with σθ isopycnals computed from the EOS-80 equation of state (Millero & Poisson
1981). EOS-80 matches the files' potential density to within about 0.006 kg m⁻³ and is
used only to draw the isopycnals.

## Derived quantities

**Mixed-layer depth** — the depth where σθ first exceeds its value at 10 m by
0.03 kg m⁻³ (de Boyer Montégut et al. 2004), interpolated between bins. Left blank where
a profile has no data in the top 15 m or never crosses the threshold.

**Chlorophyll-maximum depth** — the depth of the largest chlorophyll value in the upper
300 m after a 3-bin running mean, for profiles with data starting within 20 m of the surface.
Daytime chlorophyll fluorescence near the surface is reduced by non-photochemical quenching
(Xing et al. 2012), so daytime maxima can appear deeper than they are; compare with night
profiles using the sun strip.

Both lines are drawn as 7-profile running medians. The readout gives each profile's own value.

**Sun elevation** — computed for each profile's time and position with the low-precision
solar formulae of the Astronomical Almanac (no refraction). Classes: day > −0.833°,
civil twilight to −6°, nautical twilight to −12°, night below.

## Track distance

The distance shown for each deployment is an **estimate**: the sum of great-circle (haversine)
distances between consecutive profile positions, in time order.

* **Positions are not GPS fixes.** The gridded files (local L3 and the site's ERDDAP grids) hold
  one position per profile. A glider gets a GPS fix only when it surfaces; positions of the
  profiles in between are dead-reckoned or interpolated between fixes. The raw GPS fixes are not
  in these files, so they cannot be used here.
* **The total depends on how finely the track is sampled.** Small zig-zags between consecutive
  profiles, some real and some position error, add up. For stenella-20261103 (real-time data to
  16 Nov 2026), using every profile gives 276 km, one position per hour 263 km, one every 6 h
  219 km and one every 12 h 206 km. For the 16 Antarctic deployments, using every 2nd profile
  gives totals 3–13% lower and every 5th profile 7–27% lower.
* **It is distance over ground**, including drift with currents, not distance through the water.
* **It can differ from a pilot's figure** (for example the distance reported by SFMC), which may
  use GPS fixes, a different time span or a different method.

The average per day is the total distance divided by the time from the first to the last
profile, so it includes any pauses or gaps in the deployment.

## Bathymetry and land

GEBCO Compilation Group (2026) *GEBCO_2026 Grid*, 15 arc-second,
doi:[10.5285/4f68d5c7-45eb-f999-e063-7086abc036fa](https://doi.org/10.5285/4f68d5c7-45eb-f999-e063-7086abc036fa).

Each region uses its own subset of the GEBCO_2026 grid, downloaded for that region's area
(Antarctic Peninsula, Hawaii, California). A deployment uses the grid that covers at least 95%
of its profile positions; if none does, it is shown without seafloor or land. The viewer's
sidebar shows the grid's source and resolution under the seafloor controls.

Seafloor depth under the track is the nearest grid cell; the 3D surface is thinned for
speed. GEBCO is partly interpolated away from survey lines and is not for navigation.

## Ocean currents on the real-time map

The [Real-time](realtime.qmd) page maps the gliders that are out now (last data within 14 days)
with ocean currents around each one, refreshed by each site build.

**Model forecast.** Daily-mean currents from the Copernicus Marine Service global ocean
analysis and forecast (1/12°, 10-day forecast; product GLOBAL_ANALYSISFORECAST_PHY_001_024,
doi:10.48670/moi-00016), for yesterday (analysis) to five days ahead, in a box about ±1.25° of
latitude around each glider. The depth slider shows the mean current from the surface down to
the chosen depth, weighted by the thickness of each model level; 0 m shows the top model level.
It starts at 100 m and goes down to each glider's dive depth (90th percentile of the deepest
sample of its last 30 profiles). A glider is carried by the current averaged over its whole
dive, weighted by the time spent at each depth, so the mean down to the dive depth, given in
each glider's pop-up, is the better guide to drift; the 0–100 m mean shows where the strong
near-surface flow is. Daily means remove most of the tidal flow.

**Second model for the West Coast.** For gliders off the US West Coast the map can also show
NOAA's West Coast Operational Forecast System (WCOFS; a ROMS model, about 4 km), from the
regular-grid output on NOAA CO-OPS' THREDDS server: the newest 03Z run's nowcast (previous 24 h)
and 72-hour forecast, 3-hourly on fixed depth levels, averaged to daily means (days with at least
6 of 8 time steps) so it can be compared with the Copernicus layer. Copernicus is the default
because it covers every region; switch models in the map panel. The glider pop-up lists both
models, so you can see where the two forecasts disagree.

**Observed.** Surface currents from the US West Coast HF radar network (6 km grid; CORDC,
Scripps Institution of Oceanography, served by NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP), averaged over the last
24 hours, where a glider is inside the radar coverage. HF radar measures roughly the top
2.4 m of the ocean and reaches a limited distance offshore; there is no HF radar near the
Antarctic Peninsula.

**Measured by the glider.** Each real-time dataset on the IOOS Glider DAC carries the glider's
own depth-averaged current (`u`, `v`): the drift between the position the glider predicts from
its flight model and the GPS fix when it surfaces, divided by the time underwater. It is one
value per dive, averaged over the dive's depth and time, so compare it with the models' mean
down to the dive depth (in the glider pop-up), not with the 0–100 m mean. Being derived from the
flight model, it carries that model's errors. The map shows one purple arrow per dive for the
last 7 days, at `lat_uv`/`lon_uv` where those are filled and at the profile position otherwise.
Values that cannot be real are left off and the panel says why: `u` equal to `v` for nearly
every dive, or every value below 1 cm/s.

Arrows are drawn every 2nd model cell (about 1/6°); colour and length show speed.

## Satellite SST and chlorophyll

The real-time map can show satellite sea surface temperature or chlorophyll around each glider
for the last 7 days, and the glider pop-up puts the satellite value at the glider next to the
glider's own near-surface value for the day chosen.

**SST** is MUR v4.1 (NASA JPL; 0.01°, daily), read every 2nd pixel from the NOAA CoastWatch
ERDDAP. It is a gap-free analysis of *foundation* temperature (below any daytime surface
warming): under cloud it is filled from microwave sensors (about 25 km, and not usable near
coasts or the ice edge), other days and in-situ data, so near the Antarctic Peninsula in cloudy
weather it is largely interpolated. The pop-up shows MUR's own estimated error with the value.
If the CoastWatch server refuses the request, the map uses OSTIA (UK Met Office, 0.05°,
daily, gap-free foundation SST) from Copernicus Marine instead, and the Sources line says so.
The glider value is the mean of the 0–5 m bin over that UTC day's profiles, or of 0–10 m on days
with no data above 5 m (decimated real-time data often start around 6–10 m); the pop-up shows
which.

**Chlorophyll** is Copernicus-GlobColour, multi-sensor, 4 km, daily, near real time. The map
draws the gap-free (L4) field; pixels a satellite actually saw that day (in the observed-only
L3 field on the same grid) are opaque and pixels filled by interpolation under cloud are
faint. At the glider the value comes from observed pixels within 5 km where there are any,
and the pop-up says whether it was observed or interpolated. The glider value is the mean of the
0–10 m bins over that day's night profiles (sun below the horizon), since daytime fluorescence
is lowered by non-photochemical quenching. Expect differences: the satellite sees only the top
optical depth, misses subsurface chlorophyll maxima, uses a different method (ocean colour vs
fluorescence), and in the Southern Ocean has few clear views.

Satellite positions are each day's median glider position (night positions for chlorophyll),
and the median of the satellite pixels within 5 km of it.

### On the curtain pages

When Temperature or Chlorophyll is selected, a strip above the section shows one value per UTC
day for the whole deployment: the glider (black line; same depths and night rule as above) and
the satellite at the glider's position that day (dots). This is done for every deployment, old
and new.

- **SST:** MUR (2002 to now), with its analysis error as the error bar.
- **Chlorophyll:** only pixels a satellite actually saw that day (Copernicus-GlobColour L3,
  4 km): the reprocessed multi-sensor series first, then the near-real-time multi-sensor series,
  then the near-real-time OLCI series. Gap-filled values are not used here. Days with no clear
  pixel within 5 km are counted as "no clear view". Days that no series covers yet (the
  reprocessed series runs several months behind) are fetched again on later builds.

The line above the strip counts the days with a satellite value, with no clear view, and not
fetched yet. Values are fetched once and kept; the most recent 10 days are fetched again each
day because near-real-time values are replaced.

## Data status

The badges at the top of the home and Real-time pages are written by each site build: when the
build ran, the newest glider data on the Glider DAC (green when less than a day old, yellow
when less than 3 days, grey when older), and the newest day of satellite SST and chlorophyll on
the site. A "problems" badge and a line under them appear when the Glider DAC could not be
reached, a dataset could not be updated, or MUR SST was not available. Times are US Pacific.
The last-commit badge in the page footer shows the latest change to the site's code.

## Regions and projects

Each deployment is assigned to a region by its median position, using the lat/lon boxes in
`regions.json` in the site's repository: Antarctic Peninsula, Hawaii, and California split at
36°N into Northern and Southern California (so each opens zoomed in on its own tracks). The
overview map opens on the region with the most recent data; the buttons above it switch
region, and `?region=<name>` (or `?region=All`) in the page address opens a given one. The project is taken from the `project` attribute in
the deployment's NetCDF file and shown with a short label from `projects.json` in the
site's repository (for example "CalCOFI Survey Augmentation" → "CalCOFI Augmentation"); the
full name is shown on the deployment page. Projects not in that list are shortened to the text
before any colon.

## Colour maps

cmocean perceptually uniform colour maps (Thyng et al. 2016): *thermal* for temperature,
*haline* for salinity, *algae* for chlorophyll (log scale by default), *deep* for oxygen,
*matter* for CDOM and *turbid* for 700 nm backscatter (log scale by default).
